explanation_text: On a Zhuangjin loom, the value a thread has in the finished cloth depends entirely on which row and column of the warp-and-weft grid it sits in, the same way a digit's value depends on its place in a number. Move a thread to a new position and the pattern changes; move a digit to a new place and the value changes. The grid of the brocade is a picture of place value at work.
image_prompt: Illustrate a Zhuangjin brocade loom with woven rows labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how each thread's grid position changes the design, just as a digit's place changes its value.

explanation_text: When villagers add a basket of new fish to a village fish pond, the total count grows; when some are caught for a festival meal, the count shrinks. Addition and subtraction describe exactly these kinds of changes to a group.
image_prompt: Show a village fish pond with fish being added from a bamboo basket (labeled +) and other fish being caught (labeled -), with the pond's count changing.

explanation_text: A dragon boat's rowers sit in equal rows, so finding the total crew is repeated addition, or multiplication. Splitting the crew evenly among the rows shows division as sharing into equal groups.
image_prompt: Show a dragon boat with rowers arranged in equal rows of four, illustrating repeated addition as multiplication and even sharing as division.

explanation_text: At the Sanyuesan Song Festival, singers often perform call-and-response in pairs. When every singer has a partner the number is even; when one singer stands alone the number is odd.
image_prompt: Show Sanyuesan singers paired up across the festival stage, with one single singer left alone to show an odd number.

explanation_text: As a bowl of five-colored sticky rice is scooped out a grain at a time, counting every fifth grain by fives is a quick way to find the total. Skip counting jumps over numbers in a steady rhythm, like tapping out a pattern.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of five-colored sticky rice with grains circled in groups of five, illustrating counting by fives.

zhuang_culture: Karst peaks along the Li River
explanation_text: The karst peaks rising along the Li River come in many heights, so visitors compare them to find the tallest and the shortest. Comparing numbers works the same way, ordering values from least to greatest.
image_prompt: Show a row of karst peaks along the Li River at different heights, with > and < symbols placed between them.

explanation_text: Before the harvest, a farmer glances across the Longji rice terraces and estimates the yield will be about a hundred bundles. Rounding and estimation let us work with convenient, close numbers instead of exact counts.
image_prompt: Show a farmer looking over the Longji rice terraces and estimating about 100 bundles, with an 'about 100' label.

explanation_text: Five-colored sticky rice is dyed in five colors, so when the colors are equal each one is one fifth of the whole bowl. A fraction names one part of a whole, just as one color names one part of the festival rice.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of five-colored sticky rice divided into five equal colored sections, each labeled 1/5.

explanation_text: Cutting a round glutinous rice cake into two equal halves, then cutting each half again, gives four equal quarters. Two quarters are the same amount as one half, so 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a leaf-wrapped glutinous rice cake cut first into halves and then into quarters, with 1/2 and 2/4 marked as equal.

explanation_text: Two small bamboo baskets that each hold a quarter of the harvest can be poured into one large basket that holds half. Reducing 2/4 to 1/2 is simplifying a fraction to its simplest form.
image_prompt: Show two small bamboo baskets of rice being combined into one larger basket, labeled as 2/4 simplifying to 1/2.

zhuang_culture: Full baskets and a partial basket
explanation_text: After the harvest, a household has three full bamboo baskets of rice and one half-full basket. Writing that total as 3 and 1/2 is a mixed number, a whole amount combined with a fraction.
image_prompt: Show three full bamboo rice baskets and one half-full basket, labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: A large woven basket can hold more rice than the usual full portion, spilling past the rim. When a fraction's numerator is larger than its denominator, like 5/4, it describes more than one whole, just like the heaped basket.
image_prompt: Show a woven bamboo basket heaped with rice above its rim, labeled as 5/4 to show more than one whole.

explanation_text: After the Sanyuesan feast, leftover portions of yellow and purple rice from different bowls are poured together into one dish. Adding the fractions of the whole bowl each color represents shows how fractional parts combine.
image_prompt: Show leftover yellow and purple sticky rice from two bowls being combined into one dish, with the fractions being added.

explanation_text: If a whole serving of glutinous rice is shared and a portion is given away, the amount left is the whole minus that portion. Removing one fraction from another is fraction subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a plate of sticky rice with a portion being lifted away, the remaining amount labeled as a fraction.

explanation_text: If a child wants only half of your half-serving of sticky rice, they take one quarter of the original serving. Finding a part of a part, like 1/2 of 1/2, is multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a serving of sticky rice halved, then one half halved again to show a quarter, labeled as 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

zhuang_culture: Song sets in a festival day
explanation_text: The Sanyuesan singing lasts three hours, and each call-and-response set lasts half an hour. Finding how many sets fit, 3 divided by 1/2, gives six, which is dividing by a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a Sanyuesan schedule of three hours divided into six half-hour song sets, illustrating 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6.

explanation_text: Farmers measure the water that floods a rice paddy in liters, and paddies often need one and a half or two and a quarter liters for a section. Numbers like 1.5 and 2.25 use decimals to express amounts between whole liters.
image_prompt: Show a measuring container pouring water into a rice paddy, marked with 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters.

zhuang_culture: Half a liter of pond water
explanation_text: Whether you say half a liter or 0.5 liters of water for the seedlings, the amount is identical. Fractions and decimals are two ways to write the same quantity, and converting between them uses this connection.
image_prompt: Show two watering scoops over a rice paddy, one labeled 1/2 and the other 0.5, holding the same amount of water.

explanation_text: A student who answers 90 of 100 questions correctly on a Zhuang language quiz has scored 90 percent. Percent means out of a hundred, a way to compare parts of any whole.
image_prompt: Show a Zhuang language quiz paper marked 90/100 with a large 90% beside it.

explanation_text: At a village market, a bolt of Zhuangjin brocade is marked 20 percent off. Finding the discount means taking 20% of the original price, which is finding a percent of a number.
image_prompt: Show a market stall selling Zhuangjin brocade with a 20 percent off sign and a price tag showing the reduced amount.

explanation_text: In a Zhuang kitchen, several clay jars of rice vinegar hold amounts that no one has measured. Each unknown amount can be represented by a letter, like x, which is exactly what a variable is in math.
image_prompt: Show clay jars of rice vinegar, two labeled with amounts and one unlabeled marked with an x.

explanation_text: If you have 2 full jars of rice vinegar and one jar whose amount is unknown, the total is written as 2 + x. This combination of known numbers and a variable is a mathematical expression.
image_prompt: Show two labeled jars of rice vinegar plus one unlabeled jar, written together as 2 + x.

explanation_text: When water is carried with a bamboo shoulder pole, the two loads must balance or the pole tips. A balance shows equality, the same idea as the two sides of an equation.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo shoulder pole balanced with equal loads of water hanging from both ends, labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If the two baskets hanging from a shoulder pole are uneven, the bearer adds or removes rice from one basket until both sides balance. Finding what to add or remove to restore the balance is solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo shoulder pole with one basket sitting slightly higher, a hand adding rice to the lighter basket to balance it.

explanation_text: To make glutinous rice cakes, the rice is first pounded in a wooden mortar and then steamed. Solving a two-step equation likewise requires two actions in the right order before the answer appears.
image_prompt: Show the two steps of making rice cakes, pounding rice in a wooden mortar and then steaming it, labeled as step 1 and step 2.

explanation_text: Two terrace plots on the Longji slopes may hold different amounts of rice, so one is greater and the other is less. Inequalities record comparisons like these with > and < signs.
image_prompt: Show two rice terrace plots of different sizes with a > symbol between them and their harvest totals.

zhuang_culture: Warp before weft on the loom
explanation_text: On a Zhuangjin loom the warp threads must be set up before the weft threads can be woven through them. Some actions must happen before others, just as some operations in a math problem must be done first.
image_prompt: Show a Zhuangjin loom with warp threads being set up before weft weaving, the steps labeled in the order they must happen.

explanation_text: When a worn bamboo strut in a stilt house is replaced by a new one of the same size, the structure works exactly as before. Replacing a variable with its value in an expression is the same idea of substitution.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo stilt house frame with one strut being replaced by an identical new one, labeled as substitution.

explanation_text: Each star over the Guilin karst peaks marks one exact location in the sky. A point in geometry also marks a single, exact position, with no size of its own.
image_prompt: Show a starry sky above the karst peaks of Guilin, with individual stars highlighted as points.

zhuang_culture: Bamboo fence posts in a row
explanation_text: The straight row of bamboo fence posts around a village rice field shows what a line looks like: a straight path that goes on in both directions. Each post marks a spot along that one line.
image_prompt: Show a long straight row of bamboo fence posts beside a rice field, with arrows showing the line extending in both directions.

zhuang_culture: Dragon boat paddle in the water
explanation_text: As a dragon boat rower plunges a paddle into the river, the paddle and the water's surface form an angle. Angles measure the amount of turn between two lines, like the tilt of that paddle.
image_prompt: Show a dragon boat with a rower's paddle entering the water, the angle between paddle and surface clearly marked.

explanation_text: The tall bamboo pillars of a Zhuang stilt house stand straight up while the floor beams run across them, meeting at right angles. Perpendicular lines are lines that cross to form 90-degree angles, like these pillars and beams.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo stilt house frame with pillars and floor beams meeting at clearly marked 90° right angles.

explanation_text: The rice terraces at Longji are carved in long rows that follow the mountain's contours and never cross one another. Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet are parallel, just like those terrace rows.
image_prompt: Show the Longji rice terraces with parallel contour rows curving around the hillside, marked as parallel lines.

zhuang_culture: Panels of a village temple door
explanation_text: The carved panels of a village temple door come in closed shapes with straight sides, like rectangles and octagons. Any closed shape made of straight sides is a polygon.
image_prompt: Show a carved village temple door with rectangular and octagonal panels, highlighting the polygon shapes.

explanation_text: Rising sharply from the plain, the Guilin karst peaks trace a triangle against the sky. A triangle is a closed shape with exactly three sides, like the outline of one of those peaks.
image_prompt: Show karst peak silhouettes against the sky with one peak's triangular outline traced and labeled.

explanation_text: The woven bamboo lattice of a stilt house window is made of four-sided shapes fitted together. Any four-sided polygon is a quadrilateral, whether a square, a rectangle, or another four-sided form.
image_prompt: Show a close-up of a bamboo lattice window on a stilt house, with one four-sided unit highlighted.

explanation_text: Zhuang embroiderers stitch a border all the way around the edge of a cloth, covering the total distance of its outline. That distance around the outside of a shape is its perimeter.
image_prompt: Show a Zhuang embroidered cloth with a stitched border traced around its entire edge, marked as the perimeter.

explanation_text: Stone slabs laid to pave a village temple courtyard must cover every bit of the ground. The amount of surface a shape covers is its area, like the ground the slabs fill.
image_prompt: Show a village temple courtyard being paved with square stone slabs, the covered surface shaded to show its area.

zhuang_culture: Water held by a fish pond
explanation_text: A village fish pond can hold a certain amount of water before it overflows. The space a three-dimensional object takes up, or the amount it can contain, is its volume.
image_prompt: Show a village fish pond filled to its banks, with a cross-section showing the water it holds as its volume.

zhuang_culture: Rings of a bronze drum face
explanation_text: The face of a Zhuang bronze drum is marked with a raised sunburst of concentric circles. From the center, each ring has a radius, and a line across the whole face through the center is the diameter, properties shared by every circle.
image_prompt: Show the top face of a bronze drum with its concentric rings labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: Measured around its rim, every bronze drum's circumference is a little more than three times its diameter. That unchanging ratio, about 3.14, is pi.
image_prompt: Show a bronze drum with a measuring band around its rim and a diameter line across it, labeled with circumference, diameter, and pi.

explanation_text: Square Zhuang characters are written in a grid where every character sits in a row and a column. A coordinate plane is the same kind of grid, where each cell has a position given by its row and column.
image_prompt: Show a page of square Zhuang script characters arranged in a grid, with rows and columns labeled like a coordinate plane.

explanation_text: During the Sanyuesan festival, villagers hang lanterns along the route through the village. Marking each lantern's position on a map is plotting points, giving every spot an exact location.
image_prompt: Show a festival route with red lanterns marked as dots on a village map, each with coordinates.

explanation_text: Butterfly motifs on Zhuang embroidery are stitched so the two wings mirror each other across a center line. When one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other, the shape has symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a Zhuang embroidered butterfly with a center line splitting its two matching wings.

explanation_text: When a drum is set down, drummers turn the bronze drum until its star rays line up with the village gate. Turning a shape without changing its size is a rotation, one kind of geometric transformation.
image_prompt: Show hands turning a bronze drum so its sunburst star rays align with a village gate, labeled as a rotation.

explanation_text: To make a dipping sauce, one part rice vinegar is mixed with two parts water. Comparing the amounts as 1:2 is a ratio, a way of describing how two quantities relate.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of dipping sauce made with one part rice vinegar and two parts water, labeled as the ratio 1:2.

explanation_text: When a small embroidery pattern is enlarged onto a larger cloth, every part is scaled up by the same factor so the design keeps its shape. Keeping the ratios the same while changing size is a proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small embroidery pattern beside a larger copy of it, with matching parts connected by proportion lines.

explanation_text: A dragon boat that covers 600 meters in 2 minutes travels 300 meters each minute. Describing a quantity per single unit, like meters per minute, is a unit rate.
image_prompt: Show a dragon boat racing down a river with a speed label of 300 meters per minute.

zhuang_culture: A small copy of the cliff paintings
explanation_text: Scholars record the Zuojiang Huashan rock paintings by making small copies where every figure is reduced by the same factor. A drawing that keeps every size proportional to the real thing is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show the Huashan cliff paintings beside a smaller sketched copy, with a scale legend connecting the two.

explanation_text: When a village's rice harvest rises from 100 baskets to 120 baskets, the gain of 20 is a 20 percent increase. Percent change measures how much a quantity grows or shrinks compared with where it started.
image_prompt: Show rice baskets increasing from 100 to 120 with a +20% label above them.

explanation_text: Researchers visit the Zuojiang Huashan rock paintings and tally every painted figure, noting each one's size and pose. Gathering and recording counts like these is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a researcher at the Huashan cliff paintings tallying the painted figures on a clipboard.

explanation_text: A village records how many lanterns are hung at each festival of the year, from the Spring Festival to Sanyuesan. Organizing those counts into a table or a graph makes the numbers easy to compare.
image_prompt: Show a table and a graph comparing lantern counts at different Zhuang festivals.

zhuang_culture: Rice pounded in a wooden mortar
explanation_text: A villager pounds rice in a wooden mortar and notes the amount finished each minute: three, four, and five portions. Adding them and dividing by three gives four, the mean or average amount per minute.
image_prompt: Show a wooden mortar and pestle with three recorded amounts beside it, the average highlighted as the mean.

zhuang_culture: Scores at the Sanyuesan singing contest
explanation_text: When the scores of a Sanyuesan singing contest are lined up from lowest to highest, the score in the middle is the median. The median is the central value of an ordered set of data.
image_prompt: Show singing contest scores lined up in order with the middle score highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: At the Sanyuesan night, most of the lanterns hanging through the village are red. The value that appears most often in a set of data is the mode, like red among the lantern colors.
image_prompt: Show rows of festival lanterns in different colors with red appearing most often, labeled as the mode.

zhuang_culture: Stroke counts in square Zhuang characters
explanation_text: Some square Zhuang characters use only a few strokes while others use many. Subtracting the fewest from the most strokes gives the range, the spread of the data.
image_prompt: Show square Zhuang characters of varying stroke counts, with the simplest and most complex marked to show the range.

explanation_text: The Huashan paintings show figures in different poses, some with arms raised and others seated. A bar graph with one bar per pose makes it easy to see which pose appears most often.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph of Huashan painting figures grouped by pose, with a tall bar for the raised-arm figures.

zhuang_culture: Water level in the fish pond
explanation_text: A farmer measures the water level of the village fish pond each week through the year. Plotting the levels and joining them with a line shows the changes over time in a line graph.
image_prompt: Show a line graph of a fish pond's water level across the months, with a measuring stick and the pond beside it.

explanation_text: A bowl of five-colored sticky rice holds five colors in equal shares. A pie chart cuts a circle into slices just like the rice is split into colors, each slice showing its fraction of the whole.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart with five equal slices colored like five-colored sticky rice, beside a real bowl of the rice.

zhuang_culture: Picking a grain of red sticky rice
explanation_text: If a bowl of five-colored sticky rice holds equal numbers of all five colors, reaching in without looking gives each grain a 1 in 5 chance of being red. Probability measures how likely an outcome is.
image_prompt: Show a hand reaching into a bowl of five-colored sticky rice, with a label showing a 1 in 5 chance of picking red.

explanation_text: In Zhuang mountain songs, the lead singer's line is answered by a chorus line in a repeating back-and-forth pattern. Repeating sequences like these, whether in song or in numbers, are patterns.
image_prompt: Show two rows of folk singers trading call-and-response lines, with the repeating ABAB song pattern highlighted.

explanation_text: On the tianqin, a Zhuang stringed instrument, each fret position produces one specific pitch when the string is pressed. That rule, one input giving one output, is exactly what a function does.
image_prompt: Show a tianqin with its frets, each labeled with a pitch, illustrating how one fret position gives one note.
